evidence.claim: The Delaware River Scenic Byway follows Route 29 between Frenchtown and the riverbank tunnel in Trenton.
evidence.quote: The Delaware River Scenic Byway extends from the Route 29 tunnel in Trenton to the Uhlerstown-Frenchtown Bridge in Frenchtown.

evidence.claim: For much of the drive, both the Delaware and the Delaware and Raritan Feeder Canal are visible, with farm fields, forests and cliffs along the way.
evidence.quote: The Delaware River and the Delaware and Raritan Feeder Canal are visible for much of the drive as the Byway passes by the State Capitol and through the historic riverside towns of Titusville, Lambertville, Stockton, Raven Rock and Frenchtown, and the scenic landscape of farm fields, forests and cliffs.

evidence.claim: New Jersey DOT lists its historic, recreational and scenic qualities and gives its length as approximately 34 miles.
evidence.quote: Intrinsic qualities: Historic, recreational and scenic Length: Approximately 34 miles

evidence.claim: The road began as part of the Delaware River Drive legislated in 1911, a proposed state highway extending north from Trenton to the New York border.
evidence.quote: The current route was originally legislated in 1911 as part of the Delaware River Drive, a named state highway that was proposed to run from along the Delaware River from Trenton north to the New York border in Montague Township.

evidence.claim: Route 29 initially turned toward Newark; the 1953 renumbering redirected it from Lambertville to Frenchtown over former Route 29A.
evidence.quote: In 1953, Route 29 was shifted to follow the alignment of Route 29A to avoid the concurrencies with the U.S. Routes.

evidence.claim: Route 29 initially turned toward Newark
evidence.quote: Route 29 was initially designated in 1927 to run from downtown Trenton northeast to Newark

evidence.claim: redirected it from Lambertville to Frenchtown over former Route 29A.
evidence.quote: Route 29 was redefined to continue north from Lambertville to Frenchtown on Route 29A

evidence.claim: In Trenton, freeway construction in the 1950s filled the old Trenton Water Power Canal, using its right of way for part of the highway.
evidence.quote: From just south of Calhoun Street north to I-295, Route 29 utilized the right-of-way of what remained of the Trenton Water Power Canal, a 19th century waterway utilized by the mills of Trenton for water power. The freeway's construction resulted in the filling of the canal

evidence.claim: freeway construction in the 1950s
evidence.quote: This road was built between 1954 and 1957

evidence.claim: This corridor became the first New Jersey Scenic Byway in 1996 and gained national designation in 2009.
evidence.quote: This Byway became the first New Jersey Scenic Byway when it was designated in 1996 and it became one of two New Jersey Byways that were nationally designated in 2009.

evidence.claim: Travel south from Frenchtown through Raven Rock and Stockton to Lambertville, then Titusville and Washington Crossing State Park.
evidence.quote: historic riverside towns of Titusville, Lambertville, Stockton, Raven Rock and Frenchtown

evidence.claim: Titusville and Washington Crossing State Park.
evidence.quote: Route 29 continues north along the Delaware River through Titusville, passing by Washington Crossing State Park.

evidence.claim: North of the Scudder Falls Bridge interchange, River Road is a two-lane surface road beside the canal.
evidence.quote: Upon crossing the Delaware and Raritan Canal, Route 29 becomes a two-lane surface road known as River Road.

evidence.claim: North of the Scudder Falls Bridge interchange
evidence.quote: just to the east of the Scudder Falls Bridge.

evidence.claim: Toward Trenton, the route becomes a mix of boulevard and expressway.
evidence.quote: Between the southern terminus and I-295 in Ewing Township, the route is a mix of expressway and boulevard that runs along the Delaware River through Trenton.

evidence.claim: The State Capitol is visible from Route 29 before the byway ends at the tunnel.
evidence.quote: The State Capitol, visible from Route 29

evidence.claim: Watch for the feeder canal between the highway and the Delaware River.
evidence.quote: the Delaware and Raritan Canal, which runs between Route 29 and the river.

evidence.claim: The hamlet’s namesake rock outcrop marks the southwest corner of the Hunterdon Plateau.
evidence.quote: The rock outcrop for which it is named is the southwest corner of the Hunterdon Plateau.

evidence.claim: Bulls Island links two states by a steel suspension footbridge across the Delaware.
evidence.quote: Bull's Island Recreation Area is a forested island in the Delaware River with access to Pennsylvania by a historic steel suspension pedestrian bridge.

evidence.claim: The Lumberville–Raven Rock crossing connects the island with Lumberville, Pennsylvania; it carried road traffic from 1856 to 1944.
evidence.quote: The bridge, formerly a road bridge from 1856 to 1944, connects Bulls Island Recreation Area to Lumberville, Pennsylvania.

evidence.claim: Another transport route changed its purpose here too.
evidence.quote: the right of way was repurposed for a recreational rail trail

evidence.claim: Passenger trains served Raven Rock until 1952, and freight continued until the line closed in 1978.
evidence.quote: From 1852 to 1952 the Pennsylvania Railroad operated a passenger stop in Raven Rock via their Belvidere Division. This segment of the railroad continued to be used for freight until 1978

evidence.claim: In the early 1980s, the railway right of way became a recreation trail.
evidence.quote: the right of way was repurposed for a recreational rail trail in the early 1980s.

evidence.claim: The D&R Canal Trail runs through the surrounding park on the former railroad bed.
evidence.quote: The surrounding park includes a portion of the D&R Canal Trail, a multi-use trail built on the former Belvidere-Delaware Railroad bed

evidence.claim: A grist mill from 1877 and a linseed oil mill from 1790 are among the buildings at Prallsville Mills.
evidence.quote: an 1877 grist mill, a 1790 linseed oil mill

evidence.claim: The feeder canal reached the community in the 1830s, followed by the Belvidere-Delaware Railroad along the canal in the 1850s.
evidence.quote: The feeder canal for the Delaware and Raritan Canal, which runs along the Delaware River, was built through the community in the 1830s. Later, in the 1850s, the Belvidere-Delaware Railroad was built along the canal

evidence.claim: The property became part of the state park in 1973.
evidence.quote: The entire property became part of the D & R Canal State Park in 1973.

evidence.claim: When New Jersey could not fund restoration, local residents formed the Delaware River Mill Society in 1976.
evidence.quote: In 1976 when the State of New Jersey was unable to fund the restoration of its newly acquired Prallsville Mills, local citizens formed the Delaware River Mill Society

evidence.claim: The society remains responsible for restoring, maintaining and operating the mill complex and John Prall Jr. House.
evidence.quote: The Delaware River Mill Society is a private non-profit organization responsible for the restoration, maintenance, and operation of the historic John Prall Jr. House and the Prallsville Mills Complex

evidence.claim: The mill district now serves as an open-air museum within Delaware and Raritan Canal State Park.
evidence.quote: The area is part of the Delaware and Raritan Canal State Park and serves as open-air museum.

evidence.claim: Johnson's Ferry was the New Jersey landing for Washington and 2,400 Continental Army soldiers crossing the Delaware overnight on December 25–26, 1776.
evidence.quote: This is where George Washington and a 2,400-man detachment of the Continental Army crossed the river overnight on December 25, 1776, and into the morning of December 26, 1776

evidence.claim: Across the Delaware, the corresponding Pennsylvania landing was known as McConkey's Ferry.
evidence.quote: The corresponding ferry on the Pennsylvania side of the Delaware River was known as McConkey's Ferry.

evidence.claim: They were preparing a surprise attack on Trenton.
evidence.quote: to make a surprise attack on Trenton

evidence.claim: The Johnson Ferry House was both an 18th-century farmhouse and tavern, owned by ferry operator Garret Johnson.
evidence.quote: The Johnson Ferry House, an 18th-century farmhouse and tavern near the Delaware River, was owned by Garret Johnson

evidence.claim: ferry operator Garret Johnson
evidence.quote: who operated a 490-acre (2.0 km2) plantation and a ferry service across the Delaware.

evidence.claim: Several rooms contain period furnishings, and an 18th-century kitchen garden has been planted.
evidence.quote: Several rooms are furnished with period pieces, and an 18th-century kitchen garden has been planted.

evidence.claim: The park museum follows the campaign through the battles of Trenton, Assunpink Creek and Princeton, with a collection of American and British military artifacts.
evidence.quote: crossed the Delaware River, and fought at the Battle of Trenton, the Battle of the Assunpink Creek, and the Battle of Princeton.  It features the Harry Kels Swan Collection of Revolutionary War artifacts. Over 700 military items from the American and British Armies are included in the collection.
